newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Euro pact boosts stocks, bonds and dollar.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Euro pact boosts stocks, bonds and dollar.

text.p: European markets strove to put last week's volatility behind them on Monday as bourses, bonds and the dollar gained from agreement on an EU stability pact.
A deal between European Union leaders in Dublin on a mechanism for ensuring monetary discipline after the launch of a single currency in 1999 boosted bond markets and the dollar.

That, in turn, helped stock markets recover ground after last week's volatility and European bourses looked set to be joined by a firm Wall Street opening following news of a merger between aerospace giants Boeing and McDonnell Douglas.

Investors remained wary after the recent market turmoil, however, and traders forecast the mood would remain cautious ahead of Tuesday's meeting of the U.S. Federal Open Market Committee, which sets U.S. interest rates.
The Dublin stability deal pact was seen by the foreign exchange market as weakening sentiment for the mark and the dollar rose more than half a pfennig in early European trade.

Analysts said the pact bolstered optimism that Europe's single currrency project would go ahead on time in 1999 and increased the chance of a broad-based monetary union that would include Italy and Spain.
The pact was also seen lowering Europe's interest rate horizon, thereby buoying the dollar and yen against European currencies.
"The initial market reaction to the stability pact has been negative for the mark and this is totally justified in my opinion," said Tony Norfield, treasury economist at ABN Amro.
Government bond markets gained on the news from Dublin, with German bunds getting an added boost from an unexpected dip in an influential German business confidence index.

Europe's major stock markets -- London, Paris and Frankfurt -- all shot higher at the start, although traders said they remained vulnerable to the volatility sparked by Wall Street over the past 10 days.
Germany's 30-share DAX index zoomed 50 points, or nearly 1.8 percent, and was standing at 2,849.45 by 1215 GMT.

Wall Street's rebound from big losses on Friday to end one point up gave support to jittery European bourses, which have been watching U.S. markets closely since Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan caused turmoil earlier this month with his comments about "irrational exuberance".
Europe's largest equity market, London, climbed strongly in early business, dragged upwards by strong bond futures, the stability pact and Wall Street.
Prices began to slip after the opening impetus, however, and by 1215 GMT the FTSE 100 index was off its highs at 3,987.2, a rise of 14.8 points.

As calm returned to the market, traders said a year-end rally was still on the cards although gains were likely to be capped by worries over the strength of sterling and the prospect of a general election early in 1997.

"I think we could have a bit of a Christmas run and there has been a bit of a squeeze in some stocks today, but I am not particularly bullish with the political background we have got," said one senior trader.
French shares traded sharply higher after Friday's fall, like other European bourses gaining from bond futures.
Despite that, traders said they expected investors to remain cautious ahead of monetary meetings this week in France, the United States and Germany.
Luxury goods trader LVMH was the biggest early gainer on the CAC-40 index, rising 2.38 percent to 1,288 before slipping back for a gain of about 1.7 percent.
CURRENCIES AT 1215 GMT
The dollar was quoted around 1.5546 marks and 113.84 yen compared with 1.5473 and 113.95 in late European business on Friday.
STOCK MARKETS AT 1215 GMT
LONDON - The FTSE 100 index of top British shares was up 14.8 points at 3,987.2.
PARIS - The CAC-40 share index was up 22.71 points at 2,226.12.
FRANKFURT - The 30-share DAX was up 49.74 points at 2,849.45.
PRECIOUS METALS
Gold fixed at $368.60 vs $369.00 on Friday afternoon and a $369.55 London close. Silver lost one cent to $4.82.
